**My Reasoning:**

I've been farming this land in Quzhou for most of my life. The North China Plain tells you what to grow — winter wheat and summer maize, one rotation, same land, every year. That's what the soil here knows, that's what the market wants, and at 72 my body knows the rhythm of it too.

I have about 8 mu of contracted land. My son helps during harvest, but I manage the rest myself. I won't expand — I know my limits now. I'll stick with my 8 mu, rotating wheat into maize as I always have.

For wheat, I'll use an improved variety — probably a Jimai series adapted to Hebei conditions. Better disease resistance than traditional seed, and I've seen the yields hold up even in dry years. I apply fertilizer in split doses: base fertilizer before planting, then topdressing at jointing. I use rotary tillage after the maize harvest to break up the stubble before sowing.

For maize, I go with hybrid seed —郑单958 or whatever the county agricultural station recommends this year. I direct-seed after the wheat harvest with minimal tillage to save time and moisture. Maize gets more nitrogen because the yield response is strong.

I irrigate carefully. Quzhou's water table has been dropping my whole life. I know I should irrigate less, but the crops still need it — wheat gets 3 irrigations, maize gets 2 if the summer rains cooperate.

Pesticides: I apply what's needed, no more. Two applications for each crop — one preventive, one if I see pressure.

Fertilizer rates are moderate — split-applied nitrogen, adequate phosphorus and potassium at planting — reflecting my experience that excess inputs waste money without improving yields. I irrigate wheat three times and maize twice, keeping water use as low as I can manage given the declining groundwater table I have watched my whole life. Rotary tillage after maize prepares the seedbed for wheat; I direct-seed maize with no-tillage to save time and soil moisture. Two pesticide applications per crop keep disease and pest pressure manageable without excess.
